source.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Medical Image Representation Learning
source.authors: Philipp Wesp; Robbie Holland; Vasiliki Sideri-Lampretsa; S. Gatidis

page_placements.theme: Reconstruction and proxy metrics do not establish semantic recovery

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse autoencoders as an interpretability method for medical vision models. Its results evaluate that application, rather than testing toy-model superposition, capacity pressure in LLMs, or whether SAE features are stable canonical units.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition as background and applies SAEs to frozen medical-image embeddings. The reported SAE reconstruction, interpretability, retrieval, and performance results are included below as findings about SAE features in this setting; they do not test the listed claim versions. Configuration values used to select or rank settings are not recorded as separate rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains Matryoshka SAEs on medical vision foundation-model embeddings as an interpretability tool and reports how well that tool performs: reconstruction, downstream AUC recovery, retrieval and LLM-judged concept matching. It does not test toy-model superposition, capacity-driven or other polysemanticity, or multi-dimensional features. V4 names LLMs, and these are vision models. It does not assess whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical (V5). Toy Models of Superposition is cited only as background.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The record should also say the authors find DINOv3 produces more monosemantic features than BiomedParse. They suggest representational richness matters more than domain alignment for interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains Matryoshka SAEs with BatchTopK sparsification on frozen medical vision-model embeddings; it does not reproduce the toy-network feature-geometry experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differences by foundation model and SAE configuration; DINOv3 scores higher on monosemanticity, while the optimal DINOv3 configuration has a monosemanticity–performance trade-off. Retrieval quality varies with fingerprint size k.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs reconstruct random-weight BiomedParse embeddings with an R2 range (0.587–0.915) comparable to learned models, yet downstream AUC is only 0.606–0.651.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction fidelity alone does not show that recovered sparse features reflect learned semantic structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned models give higher SAE monosemanticity scores than the random-weight control. DINOv3 scores higher than the domain-specific BiomedParse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature interpretability in vision FMs depends on learned representational structure and differs by model.

fits_no_version.finding: Few-feature sparse fingerprints preserve most dense retrieval similarity, and LLM-judged concept matching is well above chance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features on medical vision embeddings are compact and language-describable.

record.problems: The authors describe the concept scoring as proxy-based and say expert evaluation is needed. The language-driven retrieval demonstration is a single-query proof of concept. The dataset covers normal anatomy, excludes pathological cases, and uses 2D slices rather than volumes. The study does not report uncertainty estimates for the listed results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity-versus-dimension transition, or feature geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity-allocation analysis.
No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
Sparse dictionary features are recovered only in vision FMs (BiomedParse, DINOv3), not LLMs. Feature spreading across neurons is not measured.
No completeness, cross-seed or cross-size stability, or canonicality tests. Monosemanticity is a proxy organ-label score, and cross-FM concept similarity is left to future work.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Top-N feature performance recovery: with N=10 features, BiomedParse recovers 87.8% and DINOv3 82.4% of dense ROC-AUC.
Matryoshka level statistics: median activation frequency drops across levels, and most above-null coherent features sit at the deepest level (2,610/3,682 BiomedParse; 2,361/3,577 DINOv3).

record.verdict_notes: Rows correctly link to none. The states on none-linked rows carry no version meaning. No verdicts are given because no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test toy networks, feature sparsity versus dimensionality, overlapping or nearly orthogonal directions, or regular geometric transitions.
It does not test neuron polysemanticity as a consequence of capacity competition, nor whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
It does not test polysemanticity in neurons or whether it arises without capacity pressure.
The models are medical vision foundation models, not LLMs; the study does not measure LLM feature spreading across neurons or test the stated LLM evidence.
The study evaluates SAE reconstruction and concept interpretability, but does not establish that SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
It does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.
